figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Performance versus context length. Mean score over eight benchmarks against the geometric mean of document tokens given to a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder. Memorilla lies on the Pareto frontier (dashed) with the highest score at 16 memory tokens, 394$\times$ fewer than full context.
figures.headline: Memorilla has the highest mean score across eight benchmarks at 16 memory tokens, 394× fewer than full context.
citing_sentences: Our benchmarks mirror three settings in which deployed LLMs need memory (Figures 1 and 3).
Memorilla outperforms all baselines on average while using 394$\times$, 113$\times$ and 49$\times$ fewer document tokens than full context, RAG-50 and MemoRAG in geometric mean (Figure 1).
Figure 1 places each method at the geometric mean of these counts over the eight benchmarks, and the compression column of Table 11 divides the Full Context count by the 16 tokens of Memorilla.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Memorilla architecture. A frozen encoder embeds source documents (User Chats) once into a persistent memory store. For each Query, K query-conditioned slots attend over the store and are projected into the frozen LLM’s embedding space as a memory readout.
figures.headline: Documents are encoded once into a store, and query-conditioned slots are projected into the frozen LLM's input embedding space.
citing_sentences: Here we introduce Memorilla, a memory system that learns to retrieve query-relevant information from document embeddings directly into the input embedding space of a frozen LLM (Figure 2).
Figure 2 summarizes the architecture.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Per-benchmark performance versus context length. Primary-metric score against mean document tokens per query, with a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder. Memorilla lies on the Pareto frontier (dashed) of every benchmark, leads on five and is second on NarrativeQA and PV4.
figures.headline: Memorilla lies on the Pareto frontier of every benchmark, leading on five of eight and second on two.
citing_sentences: Our benchmarks mirror three settings in which deployed LLMs need memory (Figures 1 and 3).
Figure 3 breaks this down by benchmark, where Memorilla leads on five and and is second on NarrativeQA and PV4.
On FactKG (Figure 3(a)), Memorilla reaches 84.33% against 80.43% for full context, 80.38% for MemoRAG and 78.98% for xRAG, with 108$\times$ and 36$\times$ fewer tokens than the first two.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Per-question breakdowns against RAG-50. (a) NarrativeQA question types are the question’s first word. Conceptual questions (‘Why’, ‘How’, ‘What’) favor Memorilla whereas entity-recall questions (‘Which’, ‘Who’) favor RAG. (b) Memorilla’s advantage grows with entity count, indicating better capture of multi-entity relational patterns. (c) RAG-50 degrades as more facts are composed, while Memorilla remains stable across all depths.
figures.headline: Memorilla's advantage over the retrieval baseline grows with entity count and composed facts, while retrieval wins on who and which questions.
citing_sentences: Figure 4(a) breaks down NarrativeQA performance by question type.
On FactKG, Memorilla’s advantage over RAG-50 grows monotonically with entity count, from +4.23pp at 1 entity to +7.59pp at 4+ (Figure 4(b)).
RAG-50 drops from 78.73 to 51.75 as the number of composed facts increases from 1 to 4, while Memorilla remains in the 80–89 range (Figure 4(c)).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Per-question complementarity between Memorilla and RAG-50. Share of questions answered by each method alone and by at least one of them (union), an oracle upper bound for a hybrid system. The union exceeds either method on every benchmark. †A question counts as answered when its ROUGE-L is at least $\max(0.20,m)$, where $m$ is Memorilla’s median.
figures.headline: The union of Memorilla and retrieval answers exceeds either method alone on every benchmark.
citing_sentences: In Figure 5, we show that the union of Memorilla and RAG (which is an oracle upper bound), could lead to substantial gains in performance than either approach alone, which motivates the design of hybrid retrieval and latent-memory systems as potential future work.

figures.caption: Personalization Case Study. On PersonaMem-v2, Memorilla personalizes a generic query by leveraging the user’s remembered iron-deficiency anemia history, despite no lexical overlap between the question and the relevant conversation history.
figures.headline: On PersonaMem-v2, Memorilla personalizes a generic query using a remembered iron-deficiency anemia history despite no lexical overlap.
citing_sentences: Figure 6 illustrates the complementary strength in personalization, where Memorilla uses semantically relevant medical history despite no lexical overlap with the query.

figures.caption: Reinforcement-learned memory on TextWorld. (a) A frozen encoder embeds the trajectory, the trainable memory module compresses it to $K{=}8$ latents, and the frozen LLM agent acts; sparse rewards over $G{=}16$ rollouts drive a GRPO update to the memory module alone. (b) On a held-out game, ICL loops between explored rooms while (c) Memorilla reaches the goal ($\star$).
figures.headline: On a held-out TextWorld game, full-history in-context learning loops between explored rooms while trained memory reaches the goal.
citing_sentences: After each turn, Memorilla stores the completed turn as a new document and condenses the growing document embedding store into $K=8$ memory tokens placed before the prompt (Figure 7 and Appendix G).
Figure 7 illustrates this, with ICL cycling between explored rooms and never reaching the goal, while Memorilla advances to the target room.
For agentic settings, we train the memory module from environment rewards while keeping the encoder and decoder frozen (Figure 7).

abstract: Memory enables large language models (LLMs) to use information beyond their parameters, such as past user conversations, long documents, or an agent’s earlier actions. For a frozen LLM, access to this accumulated knowledge is limited to what a memory system places in its context window. However, gathering and combining relevant information needed for each query while keeping the model’s context short remains challenging for existing systems. Here we introduce Memorilla, a memory system that gathers information from an entire document collection into a fixed number of query-dependent ‘memory tokens’ for a frozen LLM. Memorilla encodes documents (such as user chats, book chapters) once into reusable embeddings, then learns to retrieve and place query-specific information in the LLM’s input embedding space. Using only 16 memory tokens, Memorilla achieves the best average performance against baselines including Mem0 and MemoRAG across benchmarks spanning personalization, long-document and knowledge-intensive question answering. Notably, on FactKG, it reaches 84.33% accuracy versus 80.43% with full-context inference, while using 108$\times$ fewer tokens to represent the source documents. Furthermore, Memorilla can facilitate continual learning in agentic systems where the document count (the agent’s past turns) increases throughout the trajectory. In a TextWorld environment, we show that Memorilla reduces the agent’s tendency to wander between rooms it has already explored, and improves its average success rate from 18.6% with full-history in-context learning to 24.2%. Overall, Memorilla aids frozen LLMs in accumulating and using knowledge effectively across long-context interactions and takes a step towards building continually learning AI systems.

sections.body: The introduction frames memory as the way a frozen LLM reaches information outside its parameters, which is limited to what a memory system places in its context. Memorilla encodes each document once with a frozen embedding model, then a trainable module attends over all stored embeddings and outputs 16 latent memory tokens per query. Reported results include 84.33% against 80.43% for full context on FactKG with 108× fewer document tokens, 18.15 ROUGE-L against 14.21 on LaMP-4 with 474× fewer, and 57.00 exact match on TriviaQA with 743× fewer. On TextWorld, the agent completes 37.5% of held-out games in at least one of three attempts, against 25.0% with full history in context. With 512 documents on one H100, latency is 0.74s against 19.9s for full context.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Memorilla gives a frozen LLM 16 query-dependent memory tokens built from a whole document collection instead of retrieved text.

sections.body: The method has three operations: encoding, storage and retrieval. A frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B encoder maps each document chunk to a vector, and the resulting store is computed once and reused for every query. For each query, a trainable memory module initializes K=16 learned slots, conditions them on the query embedding, and refines them with cross-attention blocks that read all stored documents. The slots are then projected into the LLM input-embedding space and placed before the query text, and no LLM layer is changed. Training runs in three stages: paraphrase reconstruction on 1.98 million examples, then 1.34 million examples from ten datasets, then fine-tuning on the evaluation benchmarks. The trainable module has 194,123,776 parameters.
sections.heading: Memorilla
sections.headline: Documents are encoded once, and a trainable module maps each query to K=16 soft memory tokens for a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder.

sections.body: Baselines include cosine-similarity retrieval, Mem0, MemoRAG, two latent compression methods (xRAG and ComMer, the latter via its reported results), and LLMLingua-2, a text-based prompt compression method. Baselines use a frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B encoder and a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder, and Mem0 and MemoRAG also use Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 to build their memories. The eight benchmarks cover personalization (PersonaMem-v2, LaMP-4, LaMP-7, PersonalizationV4), long-document QA (NarrativeQA, TriviaQA) and knowledge-intensive QA (FactKG, PubMedQA). Metrics are accuracy, exact match and token-level F1 for short-form QA, and ROUGE, BLEU, F1 and METEOR for generation. Decoding uses temperature 0, and the serving stack enforces a fixed decoder context limit, enabling YaRN when an assembled full-context input exceeds it.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Memorilla is compared with retrieval, compression and memory baselines on eight benchmarks using a frozen Qwen3-8B decoder.

sections.body: Memorilla has the highest mean score across the eight benchmarks, using 394×, 113× and 49× fewer document tokens than full context, RAG-50 and MemoRAG in geometric mean. On FactKG it reaches 84.33% against 80.43% for full context, and on TriviaQA it reaches 57.00 exact match against 56.60 for MemoRAG. On PersonaMem-v2 short-answer it reaches 44.60% against 30.90% for xRAG, the strongest baseline. Where memory does not help, MemoRAG leads NarrativeQA ROUGE-1 at 21.80 against 19.68, and LLMLingua-2 reaches 69.00% on PubMedQA against 59.00% for Memorilla. These leading baselines receive 18 to 690 times more document tokens. Full context trails Memorilla on 20 of 21 metrics in Table 11, so supplying every document is not an upper bound.
sections.heading: Quantitative Results
sections.headline: Memorilla has the highest average score and leads on five of eight benchmarks, with a baseline ahead on NarrativeQA, PersonalizationV4 and PubMedQA.

sections.body: On NarrativeQA, Memorilla beats RAG-50 by +4.91 ROUGE-L on why questions and +7.02 on how questions, while RAG-50 leads by +3.45 on who and +2.93 on which. One stated explanation is that compression keeps global structure but loses exact surface tokens. On FactKG, Memorilla's advantage over RAG-50 grows from +4.23pp at one entity to +7.59pp at four or more, and RAG-50 drops from 78.73 to 51.75 as composed facts rise from 1 to 4. The methods answer different questions: 15.9% of FactKG questions are answered only by Memorilla and 10.0% only by RAG-50. Both methods are biased toward judging claims false, since true claims make up 89.5% of joint errors but 28.7% of joint successes.
sections.heading: What Does Memorilla Learn?
sections.headline: Memorilla's advantage over retrieval-augmented generation (RAG-50) grows with entity count, while retrieval wins on who and which questions in NarrativeQA.

sections.body: A frozen Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 agent acts in TextWorld games of up to 65 rooms, with at most 50 turns. Memorilla stores each completed turn as a document and produces K=8 memory tokens placed before the prompt. Only the memory module is trained, from random initialization, with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on game reward. Every condition keeps the full history under the same input budget. Trained memory raises avg@3 from 0.186 to 0.242 and pass@3 from 0.250 to 0.375 relative to full-history in-context learning. Untrained memory falls below that baseline on both metrics, at 0.153 and 0.225, so the gain comes from learning. The in-context baseline exhausts its 4,096-token budget on 71% of rollouts against 58% for Memorilla, and remaining failures concentrate in the longest games.
sections.heading: Continual Learning with Memorilla
sections.headline: Reinforcement-trained memory on TextWorld raises the average solve rate and cuts rollouts that exhaust the token budget.

sections.body: Memorilla keeps persistent storage separate from the per-query context, so documents can be added without updating the LLM. The conclusion reports leads on average across personalization, long-document and knowledge-intensive tasks while using fewer document tokens than the baselines. The stated limitations are that Memorilla can lose fine-grained factual details, probably because the encoder was never trained for memory compression, that only a Qwen encoder paired with a Qwen decoder was tested, and that coding domains were not evaluated. Because LLM decoding dominates latency, efficiency gains appear mainly for large collections. Each user's store can be kept on device or deleted on request, which the authors say eases privacy concerns.
sections.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
sections.headline: The learned memory interface can serve growing histories with a fixed token count, but it can lose fine-grained factual details.

sections.body: Appendix A compares textual memory, latent compression and model memory approaches. Appendix B gives the training data: about 2M paraphrase reconstruction examples from English Wikipedia, and a finetuning mixture of 1,343,993 queries across 10 sources (Table 1). Table 2 lists the chunk unit for each benchmark, Table 3 the model configuration, and Table 4 the three training stages with their optimizer settings. Figures 9 to 12 show ablations over memory-token count, inference-time token budget, comparable-budget LoRA adaptation, and encoder size. Appendix G gives the full TextWorld reinforcement-learning configuration, including a GRPO group size of G=16.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists related work, training data and configuration, benchmark details, memory-token ablations and the TextWorld reinforcement-learning setup.
